✨ Key Features
This isn't a simple script that pastes GPT output. It's a **full agentic system** with fault tolerance, parallelism, and intelligent orchestration.

chunks.title: AI LeetCode Agent · README.md · 🧠 Multi-LLM Intelligence
chunks.heading: 🧠 Multi-LLM Intelligence
chunks.text:
🧠 Multi-LLM Intelligence
The agent doesn't depend on a single AI provider. It chains **5 LLM providers** in priority order — Groq (fastest, free), OpenRouter, Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT-4o, and Ollama (fully local). When one provider hits a rate limit, quota cap, or returns an error, the system **automatically and silently** falls back to the next provider. During the 230-problem run, Groq's daily token limit was exhausted around problem #80 — the agent switched to OpenRouter mid-sentence and kept going. No crash, no restart, no human needed.

Each generated solution is also **locally verified** against the problem's test cases before submission. If the code fails locally, the agent retries with a different LLM rather than wasting a submission attempt.

chunks.title: AI LeetCode Agent · README.md · ⚡ 4x Parallel Speed
chunks.heading: ⚡ 4x Parallel Speed
chunks.text:
⚡ 4x Parallel Speed
Instead of solving one problem at a time, the agent launches **4 independent Chrome browser instances**, each running on its own debug port (9222-9225). A central orchestrator dispatches problems from a shared queue. While Worker 0 is waiting for its submission verdict, Workers 1-3 are already generating and submitting their own solutions. The result is **~4x throughput** — 4 problems solved every 30-45 seconds instead of 1.

Each worker has its own browser profile, session cookies, and error handling. If one worker crashes or times out on a hard problem, the others keep running. The orchestrator marks the failed problem and moves on — no single failure blocks the pipeline.

chunks.title: AI LeetCode Agent · README.md · 🔐 Stealth & Reliability
chunks.heading: 🔐 Stealth & Reliability
chunks.text:
🔐 Stealth & Reliability
LeetCode uses Cloudflare protection and bot detection. Traditional automation (filling login forms, clicking buttons with Selenium) gets blocked instantly. This agent takes a different approach: it **exports your real browser session cookies** and injects them directly into each Playwright Chrome instance via `context.add_cookies()`. No login form is ever touched. To LeetCode's servers, the agent looks like a regular authenticated user browsing the site.

The system also maintains persistent Chrome profiles so browser fingerprinting stays consistent across runs. A `status.json` file tracks every problem's state (pending, solved, failed), so you can stop the agent anytime and **resume exactly where you left off** — even days later.

📱 Real-Time Monitoring
Every submission generates a Telegram notification — including a **screenshot of the result page** showing "Accepted" or "Wrong Answer". You can be away from your computer (sleeping, in class, at work) and still see exactly what the agent is doing on your phone.

The Telegram bot also supports interactive commands:
- `/status` — see how many problems are solved right now
- `/run` — start a new solving session remotely
- `/stop` — gracefully stop all workers
- `/solved` — list every problem that's been accepted

All run data is also saved as structured JSON logs locally, so you have a complete audit trail of every attempt, every solution, and every result.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Overview
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Overview
Bull/Bear Autopilot

  An unattended research analyst for Indian IPOs.
  It finds every live issue, reads the prospectus, argues both sides with page
  citations,fact-checks its own arguments against the document, and delivers a
  verdict to Telegram — with no human in the loop.

  
  
  
  

---

**Why this is different from the other LLM-reads-a-PDF projects:**

- **Not a chatbot.** Nothing to prompt. It wakes on a schedule, decides what is
  worth reading, and reports.
- **Not plain RAG.** No similarity search over chunks — the prospectus becomes a
  numbered, page-cited `Fact[]` that every later stage must argue *from*.
- **Two adversaries, not one narrator.** A bull and a bear build cases from the
  same facts, so a weakness has to survive an advocate trying to bury it.
- **The eval layer is deterministic and the model cannot overrule it.** A figure
  that appears in no cited fact is `unsupported`, full stop — and confidence is
  *arithmetic* over those outcomes, never the model's own self-report.

The most important component is the one that **rejects its own output**. In the
committed sample run, the claim it threw out was the *bull's* — and the argument
was arithmetically correct. See why.

python scripts/demo_dry_run.py --offline

No API key, no network, no credential. Shows the whole pipeline's shape in about
two seconds. **Start there.**

> ⚠️ **Not investment advice.** This is a software engineering portfolio project.
> Verdicts come from a language model reading a fraction of a prospectus. See the
> full disclaimer.

---

The last one matters most for an unattended system. A pipeline that runs at 09:15
with nobody watching must never let silence look like success — which is why a

The honest version of the claim: the LLM is still doing the reading and the

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · 1. The ranker uses no LLM
chunks.heading: 1. The ranker uses no LLM
chunks.text:
1. The ranker uses no LLM
Scoring the universe is bookkeeping, not judgement. A model cannot be relied on
to order the same 23 listings the same way twice, and "why did this make the
cut?" has to be answerable in arithmetic. Every listing carries the points it
earned and a human-readable reason, and the artifact records the reasoning for
the **whole** universe — not just the shortlist — so a near-miss can be audited
without re-running discovery. Weights and the closed-issue rule are in
Ranking.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · 2. The bull and bear are citation-grounded
chunks.heading: 2. The bull and bear are citation-grounded
chunks.text:
2. The bull and bear are citation-grounded
Both agents see the same `Fact[]` and are held to the same contract: every claim
must cite `Fact.id`s, and a claim citing an id that was never issued is dropped
before it can be scored. A fabricated citation is worse than no claim. Every
figure in a claim's *text* is unioned with its declared `numbers`, so omitting a
number from the array cannot exempt it from being checked.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · 3. The fact-checker is the eval layer, and it is deterministic first
chunks.heading: 3. The fact-checker is the eval layer, and it is deterministic first
chunks.text:
3. The fact-checker is the eval layer, and it is deterministic first
Arithmetic runs before any model gets a say, and no model may overrule it. An
unmatched figure is `unsupported`, full stop. Digit boundaries are respected, so
`1250` is not "found" inside `12500` — an order-of-magnitude error is exactly the
kind of thing that must not slip through. The LLM adjudicates only the residual
qualitative band, and if it is unavailable the claim settles at `partial` rather
than being waved through. Full status table in
The fact-checker.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · 5. Seven providers, one function, no vendor SDKs
chunks.heading: 5. Seven providers, one function, no vendor SDKs
chunks.text:
5. Seven providers, one function, no vendor SDKs
Agents call `chat(messages, temperature=0.2) -> str` and never learn which
provider answered. The router cascades through whatever has a key, retries
transient failures in place and fails permanent ones over immediately. Plain REST
over `httpx`, so there is no SDK to pin. See
Multi-provider LLM access.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · 6. Autopilot with day-level dedup
chunks.heading: 6. Autopilot with day-level dedup
chunks.text:
6. Autopilot with day-level dedup
One command is the whole system, and it remembers what it already did. Dedup is
keyed on the **Indian** calendar date, because IST is UTC+5:30 and a UTC-keyed
autopilot would treat a 19:00 UTC run and the next morning's 06:00 UTC run as
different days when they are the same Indian day. Only *successes* are recorded,
so an IPO whose prospectus 404s at 06:00 is retried at noon rather than written
off. Details in Dedup.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · A sample verdict, explained
chunks.heading: A sample verdict, explained
chunks.text:
A sample verdict, explained
Committed under `data/samples/` is a real run, sanitized for
publication: the full artifact and the
rendered memo. No key needed to read either.

AVOID    conf 45%   bull 3.5 / bear 6.5   Symbiotec Pharmalab Limited
  full_drhp, 12 of 574 pages read, 24 facts extracted
  fact-check: {'supported': 9, 'unsupported': 1, 'partial': 2}

**The interesting part is the single unsupported claim, and it is the bull's.**
Arguing that the promoters were staying invested, the bull wrote that "₹18,500.00
million comes from the two Investor Selling Shareholders." The prospectus states
each investor's sale separately — ₹12,500m and ₹6,000m — but never their sum. So:

cites F0001, F0003, F0004, F0005, F0014, F0015, F0016
      — figure(s) 18500 appear in no cited fact

The arithmetic is correct. The claim is still `unsupported`, because 18,500 is
the *model's* addition and not the document's statement, and the checker has no
way to distinguish a sound inference from a hallucinated total. That strictness is
the design: it is what stops a fabricated figure from arriving with a citation
stapled to it. It also cost a defensible argument, which is the honest trade.

Because the figure was a *number* rather than a vague sentence, it was recorded in
`material_unsupported_ids` and penalised harder. The judge proposed a base
confidence of **0.58**; the pipeline derived what a human sees:

| Factor | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| base (judge's own) | 0.58 | |
| evidence quality | × 1.00 | `full_drhp` — the real prospectus was downloaded and read |
| share unsupported | × 0.92 | 1

chunks.heading: Multi-provider LLM access
chunks.text:
Multi-provider LLM access
The router cascades through providers in a fixed order and the first one that
answers wins. **Providers without a key are skipped**, so one key is enough.

| # | Provider | Default model | Env key |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Tabitoken** (third-party Claude proxy) | `claude-opus-5` | `TABITOKEN_API_KEY` |
| 2 | OpenRouter | `google/gemini-2.5-flash` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| 3 | Google Cloud Agent Platform | `gemini-2.5-flash` | `AGENT_PLATFORM_API_KEY` + `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` |
| 4 | Groq | `openai/gpt-oss-120b` | `GROQ_API_KEY` |
| 5 | Gemini (AI Studio) | `gemini-2.5-flash` | `GEMINI_API_KEY` |
| 6 | OpenAI | `gpt-4o-mini` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| 7 | OpenRouter free tier | `…gemini-2.0-flash-exp:free`, `…llama-3.3-70b-instruct:free`, `…deepseek-chat-v3-0324:free` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |

Tier 1 is first because it is the strongest model in the cascade, and analysis
quality is the whole point. It is an **OpenAI-compatible proxy at
`https://tabitoken.com`** — set the host without a path and the router appends
`/v1` itself; the domain is never rewritten. The proxy publishes four Claude
models (`claude-opus-5`, `claude-opus-5-thinking`, `claude-opus-4-8`,
`claude-opus-4-8-thinking`); the default is the strongest non-thinking one,
because this pipeline asks for JSON far more often than prose. Override with
`TABITOKEN_MODEL=` — no code change.

**Anthropic's own API is not in the cascade and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is never
read.** Claude is reached only through that proxy, which is a different vendor,
host and credential. Prompts leave your machine for a

what that means in practice. Tier 3 is likewise distinct from tier 5: enterprise

Behaviour:

- **Transient failures** (429, 5xx, timeouts) retry inside the same provider with
  exponential backoff; **permanent ones** (bad key, unknown model, malformed
  request) fail that provider immediately and move the cascade on.

  provider 404s, set `GROQ_MODEL=` in `.env` rather than editing code.
- A model that rejects JSON mode is transparently retried without it.
- The router sends an honest `User-Agent` (`Bull-Bear-Autopilot/1.0`). Some hosts

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Sources
chunks.heading: Sources
chunks.text:
Sources
| Source | Kind | Contributes |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `nse-current-issue` | JSON API | live issues: symbol, price band, share count, dates |
| `nse-upcoming-ipo` | JSON API | forthcoming mainboard issues |
| `nse-upcoming-sme` | JSON API | forthcoming SME issues |
| `chittorgarh-dashboard` | HTML table | breadth — issues NSE hasn't published yet |

Each source is an adapter behind a `Protocol`, so one can be added, reordered or
dropped without touching the discovery loop. Notes:

- **A dead source degrades the run, it never ends it.** Failures land in
  `sources_failed` and the universe is built from whatever answered. Only a total
  wipe-out (or zero listings) raises `ScoutError`.
- **Sources span two hosts** deliberately, so an NSE outage still yields a
  universe.
- **NSE's `issueSize` is a share count, not rupees.** The value in crore is
  derived as `shares × top of price band ÷ 10⁷`, which is what makes sizes
  comparable across IPOs.
- **Records are merged, not just de-duplicated.** Matching is by symbol, then by
  a normalised name (`"Tempsens Instruments (India) Limited"` and
  `"Tempsens Instruments IPO"` both key to `tempsensinstruments`). A thin record
  donates dates to a rich one, a rich one donates the symbol and size back, and
  an IPO seen on both venues becomes `Exchange.BOTH`.
- **No BSE adapter.** Every BSE endpoint probed returns an HTML block page to a
  non-browser client. Shipping a source that can't be reached would just be a
  permanent entry in `sources_failed`.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Ranking
chunks.heading: Ranking
chunks.text:
Ranking
Transparent, LLM-free and deterministic — the same universe always produces the
same order:

| Signal | Weight | Rationale |
|--------|--------|-----------|
| Issue size | 0–50, log-scaled | primary signal; log keeps one mega-IPO from drowning the rest |
| Status | open 20, upcoming 16, unknown 6 | an open issue is the most urgent |
| Exchange | both 6, single 4, unknown 0 | dual-listing implies a mainboard issue |
| Offer document linked | 8 | unlocks the whole downstream pipeline |
| Symbol known | 3 | confirmed by an exchange, not just a dashboard |
| Dates known | 3 | schedulable |
| Corroboration | 4 | reported independently by more than one source |

An IPO that can no longer be subscribed to (`closed` / `listed` / `withdrawn`) is
**sorted below every actionable listing regardless of size** — a ₹20,000cr closed
issue is worth nothing to a subscriber. Ties break on size, then the sooner
deadline, then name, so the order is total and reproducible.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Finding the offer document
chunks.heading: Finding the offer document
chunks.text:
Finding the offer document
`IPOListing.drhp_url` is almost always `None` — no discovery source publishes a
machine-readable prospectus link. So the fetch agent hunts for one, degrading in
steps rather than failing, and records every step it tried:

| Step | Source | Evidence quality |
|------|--------|------------------|
| 1 | `drhp_url` on the listing, if discovery happened to find one | `full_drhp` |
| 2 | **NSE offer-document indices** — the machine-readable index of every DRHP / RHP / prospectus NSE has received, matched by symbol then exact name | `full_drhp` |
| 3 | **Structured summary pages** — issue structure and live subscription demand, when no prospectus exists yet | `limited_source` |
| 4 | The listing itself, restated and nothing more | `metadata_only` |

Step 2 is what makes the autopilot work unattended: in the sample run it found and
downloaded a 574-page DRHP for an IPO whose `drhp_url` was `None`. Notes:

- **Zipped filings are unwrapped** — NSE serves some documents as archives.
- **Downloads are size-capped** (`FETCH_MAX_BYTES`) and a truncated document is
  refused rather than analysed, since a half-read DRHP silently loses risk factors.
- **The metadata fallback invents nothing.** It restates the discovery record and
  stops, which is why it is labelled as evidence rather than as analysis.
- **One IPO's fetch failure never ends the run.** It lands in `failures` with its
  stage, and the rest of the shortlist proceeds.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · The debate
chunks.heading: The debate
chunks.text:
The debate
Both agents see the same `Fact[]` and are held to the same contract:

- **Every claim must cite `Fact.id`s.** A claim citing an id the document agent
  never issued is dropped before the fact-checker ever sees it.
- **Every figure in a claim's text is exposed for checking.** The declared
  `numbers` are unioned with the numbers parsed out of the claim's own text, so
  omitting a figure from `numbers` cannot exempt it from being verified.
- **Fiscal period labels are not figures.** `FY26`, `Q3 FY26` and `fiscal 2026`
  are stripped first, or a perfectly grounded claim would be marked unsupported
  for citing a fact that doesn't contain the number 26.
- **The prompt advertises only figures the source text contains.** `Fact.numbers`
  is model output and sometimes glues two adjacent figures into one; reprinting
  that would invite a debater to argue a number the page never stated.
- The bear is explicitly pointed at concentration, litigation, leverage,
  offer-for-sale share, valuation and risk density — the surfaces that actually
  sink Indian IPOs — rather than being asked to be negative.
- Facts are selected to keep **every category represented** in the prompt. Plain
  truncation would hand the bear a window with no risk factors in it.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · The fact-checker is the eval layer
chunks.heading: The fact-checker is the eval layer
chunks.text:
The fact-checker is the eval layer
Deterministic first, and no model may overrule arithmetic:

| Condition | Status |
|-----------|--------|
| A figure in the claim appears in no cited fact's `numbers` **or** text | `unsupported` |
| `citation_ids` missing, empty, or naming an unknown fact | `unsupported` |
| Figures all trace, wording tracks the cited facts | `supported` |
| Qualitative claim loosely grounded in its citations | `partial` |
| Qualitative claim unrelated to its citations | `unsupported` |

Details that matter:

- **Digit boundaries are respected**, so `1250` is not "found" inside `12500`.
- **A number only in a fact's prose still counts.** `Fact.numbers` is model output
  too and routinely misses a figure.
- **One bad figure condemns the whole claim** — a claim is not partly true.
- An ungrounded *number* is recorded separately from a vague sentence, in
  `material_unsupported_ids`; the judge penalises it harder.
- The LLM adjudicates only the residual qualitative band, and if it is
  unavailable or replies unusably the claim settles at `partial`.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · The judge
chunks.heading: The judge
chunks.text:
The judge
The model rules on the verdict, scores and prose. Confidence is **not** left to
it — `adjust_confidence` derives it:

confidence = base × evidence_factor × unsupported_factor × material_penalty

| Input | Effect |
|-------|--------|
| `full_drhp` / `limited_source` / `metadata_only` | × 1.0 / 0.6 / 0.3 |
| Share of claims unsupported | × (1 − share), floored at 0.25 |
| Each ungrounded figure | × 0.85, up to four |
| A debate with nothing to check | × 0.4 |

Clamped to `[0.05, 1.0]` — never 0.00, which would read as a confident "nothing
here" rather than "we could not tell". Weak evidence also adds a caveat to the top
of `key_risks`, and a `metadata_only` memo says outright that it is **not an
analysis**.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Delivery to Telegram
chunks.heading: Delivery to Telegram
chunks.text:
Delivery to Telegram
Set both of these in `.env` and delivery works with no further setup:

| Variable | How to get it |
| --- | --- |
| `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` | Create a bot with @BotFather; it replies with the token. |
| `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID` | Message your own bot once, then read `result[0].message.chat.id` from `https://api.telegram.org/bot/getUpdates`. |

The bot cannot open a conversation with you, which is why you have to message it
first. The token is redacted in all log output — see Security.

Telegram gets the mobile summary **plus the detailed memo file, plus the company
offer document when one was fetched** — the reading and the evidence in the same
thread, so nothing has to be looked up on a laptop later. You receive one header
message (universe size, Top N, analysed ok/failed, evidence-quality counts,
sources down), then per IPO a summary message followed by its files:

| File | Comes from | Sent as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bull/bear memo | the memo this run generated | `SYMBIOTEC-bull-bear-memo.md` |
| Offer document | the DRHP/RHP that was actually read | `SYMBIOTEC-offer-document.pdf` |

Then a footer naming the artifact — basename only, never a local path — and any
partial-run flags in plain language.

Files are best-effort and the summary never waits on them. If no document was
recorded you get one line saying so; if one is over Telegram's 50 MB bot limit you
get one line and the upload is skipped. Either way the text is already delivered,
and a failed upload is reported rather than swallowed.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Scheduling it
chunks.heading: Scheduling it
chunks.text:
Scheduling it
`scripts/autopilot.py` is the portable entrypoint every scheduler runs. It puts the
project root on `sys.path`, forwards your arguments to the `autopilot` subcommand,
and exits with that subcommand's code — `0` ran as intended (including "nothing new
today"), `1` tried and failed, `2` is misconfigured.

It needs no working directory set: `.env`, `data/`, `reports/` and the state file
are all resolved from the package location, not the cwd (`app/config.py:16`). Only
a log redirect is relative, so use an absolute path for that.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Windows — Task Scheduler
chunks.heading: Windows — Task Scheduler
chunks.text:
Windows — Task Scheduler
`scripts\autopilot.cmd` is the thing to schedule. It finds the
project's own `.venv` interpreter (falling back to `python`), forces UTF-8 output,
forwards your arguments, and returns the exit code so the task history shows a
failure as a failure.

**Task Scheduler** → *Create Task*:

| Tab | Setting |
| --- | --- |
| General | name it; *Run only when user is logged on* is simplest — *whether user is logged on or not* needs the account password stored |
| Triggers | *New* → Daily → 09:15, recur every 1 day |
| Actions | *New* → *Start a program* → Program: `\scripts\autopilot.cmd` → **Start in: ``** |
| Settings | tick *Run task as soon as possible after a scheduled start is missed* |
| Conditions | on a laptop, untick *Start the task only if the computer is on AC power*; tick *Wake the computer to run this task* |

The trigger time is the machine's local clock. On an IST machine 09:15 is early
enough to beat the 10:00 IST open; elsewhere, pick the wall-clock time that lands
in the Indian morning.

**Start in** is belt and braces: every path the project reads or writes derives
from the package location, not the working directory, so the run is already
independent of where it was launched — the entrypoint does no `chdir`.

To keep a transcript of every run instead of losing it to a closed window, set
Program to `cmd.exe` and Arguments to (one line, quotes included):

/c "\scripts\autopilot.cmd >> \logs\autopilot.log 2>&1"

`logs\` is committed but its contents are gitignored, so the redirect works on day
one and never lands a run transcript in version

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Linux and macOS — cron
chunks.heading: Linux and macOS — cron
chunks.text:
Linux and macOS — cron
Run it by hand once from the activated venv before you schedule anything:

python scripts/autopilot.py --top-n 3

Then open your crontab:

crontab -e

And add one line — 09:15 daily, absolute paths throughout, output appended to the
log:

15 9 * * * /path/to/bull-bear/.venv/bin/python /path/to/bull-bear/scripts/autopilot.py --top-n 3 >> /path/to/bull-bear/logs/autopilot.log 2>&1

Three things about cron that bite people:

- **cron's `PATH` is almost empty and no venv is active**, so naming
  `.venv/bin/python` explicitly is not optional. There is no `activate` step in a
  cron job — that is why the line above uses absolute paths and no `cd`.
- **`%` is special in crontab.** Everything after the first unescaped `%` is fed to
  the command as stdin, not run as part of it. No `%` appears above; if you add one
  (a `date +%F` in the log name, say), escape it as `\%`.
- **cron does not set a locale**, so a UTF-8 stream is not guaranteed. The pipeline
  reconfigures its own streams, but a crash during import would report itself in the
  wrong encoding — the one thing the line above does *not* already handle. Add
  `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` on its own line above the schedule.

`logs/` is committed but its contents are gitignored, so the redirect works on day
one and never lands a run transcript in version control.

Check it is registered, and watch the next run:

crontab -l

tail -f /path/to/bull-bear/logs/autopilot.log

chunks.text:
~/.config/systemd/user/bull-bear.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run Bull/Bear Autopilot every morning

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 09:15:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Known limitations
chunks.heading: Known limitations
chunks.text:
Known limitations
Written down rather than smoothed over, because most of them bound how much the
verdicts are worth:

- **Only the first N pages of a DRHP are read.** The sample run read 12 of 574
  pages: the cover, capital structure and the start of the risk factors. The
  financial statements and the bulk of the litigation sections are hundreds of pages
  deeper. Verdicts from a shallow run reflect what was read, which is why the memo
  prints `pages_analyzed` alongside the ruling.
- **Weak extractors glue adjacent figures, and the eval layer charges for it.** On
  free models, `"₹1,500.00 million … face value of ₹2 each"` comes back as
  `1500.002`, and across three live runs on the same DRHP, 24% / 43% / 80% of
  declared fact numbers did not appear in the fact's own text. Glued figures are
  kept out of the debate prompt, and the parser no longer creates them itself, but a
  figure the model declares and never writes down is still checked — so confidence
  lands low on evidence that is mostly sound. **Read a low-confidence verdict as
  "the extractor was sloppy" at least as much as "the IPO is weak."** The fix is a
  stronger model, not a laxer checker.
- **A correct inference can still be marked unsupported.** If the document states
  ₹12,500m and ₹6,000m separately, a claim citing their ₹18,500m sum fails, because
  the checker cannot distinguish sound arithmetic from a hallucinated total. That is
  the intended trade — see the sample verdict — but it
  does mean `unsupported` sometimes means "unstated" rather than "wrong".
- **Free-tier token ceilings, not code,

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Security
chunks.heading: Security
chunks.text:
Security
**Never commit a real credential.** All secrets live in `.env`, which is
gitignored. `.env.example` is the committed template and contains no values — only
variable names and comments describing the shape of what goes there.

cp .env.example .env      # then fill in .env, never .env.example

Before your first push:

git check-ignore -v .env

If that prints nothing, **stop** — `.env` is not being ignored and a push would
publish it.

Assignments in `.env.example` are deliberately left **blank** rather than filled
with dummy values. Blank is how the router is told to skip a provider; a
placeholder string like `your-key-here` would make that provider fail on every
call instead of being skipped.

What the code does, enforced by tests rather than intentions:

- **Keys travel in headers, never in URLs**, because `httpx` logs every request URL
  at `INFO` and a key in a query string would land in `logs/autopilot.log`.
- **The Telegram token is redacted in log output.** It appears in the Bot API's URL
  path by design, so it is rewritten to `bot` before anything is logged.
- **Failures never print the credential** — only the status and a truncated body.
- **Run artifacts contain no credentials.** `data/runs/*.json` and `reports/*.md`
  record which provider *name and model* served each call, never the key.
- **The test suite is hermetic**, and the guard keys off field-name suffixes, so a
  newly added `*_api_key` setting is covered automatically.

chunks.title: Bull/Bear Autopilot · README.md · Why this is not plain RAG
chunks.heading: Why this is not plain RAG
chunks.text:
Why this is not plain RAG
A retrieval-augmented chatbot over a prospectus does one thing: finds passages
that look like your question and asks a model to write about them. Ask it "is
this IPO a good buy?" and you get fluent prose whose relationship to the document
is unverified — and unverifiable, because nothing in the design distinguishes a
grounded sentence from a plausible one.

Six differences, each of them structural rather than a prompt instruction:

| Plain RAG | This system |
|---|---|
| Retrieves passages similar to a query | **Extracts a numbered, page-cited `Fact[]`** — an addressable evidence base, built once and reused by every downstream stage |
| One model writes one answer | **Two adversarial agents** argue opposite sides from the *same* facts, so a weakness has to survive an advocate who is trying to bury it |
| Citations are decorative, and often unchecked | **Citations are enforced.** A claim citing an id the extractor never issued is dropped before the fact-checker sees it |
| "Grounded" means the model said so | **Every figure is re-derived mechanically.** A number in a claim that appears in no cited fact's `numbers` *or* text is `unsupported`, and no model can overrule that |
| Confidence is the model's self-report | **Confidence is arithmetic** over evidence quality and fact-check outcomes — a testable promise, not a vibe |
| A failure looks like a confident answer | **Degradation is explicit and typed.** `partial` says *what* broke — a dead source, a failed IPO, a dropped page window, thin evidence |

The last one matters most for an unattended system. A

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · 1. Goals and non-goals
chunks.heading: 1. Goals and non-goals
chunks.text:
1. Goals and non-goals
**Goals**

1. Expose an **OpenAI-compatible** `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint (streaming and non-streaming) that sits in front of two or more upstream LLMs.
2. For each request, choose a **cheap** or **strong** model so that the expected quality loss versus always using the strong model is **≤ ε**, with ε set by the operator (or the client, from a pre-calibrated grid).
3. Make the guarantee **auditable**: every calibration is a versioned, immutable artifact; every response says which calibration produced the routing decision.
4. Behave like a real gateway: bounded overhead, safe failure modes, structured logs, metrics, load-tested.

**Non-goals (MVP)**

- Per-prompt guarantees (the guarantee is marginal; see §2.3).
- Tool calls, vision, audio, or multi-turn agentic traffic in the calibrated path. These are routed to the strong model by the scope guard.
- Training or fine-tuning the LLMs themselves.
- Multi-tenant billing, SSO, or a production control plane.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · Key properties of the request path
chunks.heading: Key properties of the request path
chunks.text:
Key properties of the request path
- **Pre-generation routing.** The decision uses only the prompt (and cheap features), so streaming works unchanged: the first byte comes from the chosen model, with no buffering. Post-generation cascades (generate cheap → check → escalate) conflict with streaming and add latency, so they are a **(stretch)**.
- **Fail-safe direction.** Any internal failure (router error, missing/stale artifact, scope-guard doubt) routes to the **strong** model. Failure never silently makes the system *cheaper*.
- **Fallback only upward.** If the cheap provider errors before the first token, retry on strong (guarantee-preserving). If the strong provider is down, falling back to cheap is allowed only when the client sends `x-certiroute-allow-downgrade: true`; those responses are tagged `degraded` and excluded from the guarantee.
- **Mid-stream failure** cannot be re-routed; emit an SSE error event, log it, and count it in availability metrics.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · 5.2 Scope guard (MVP)
chunks.heading: 5.2 Scope guard (MVP)
chunks.text:
5.2 Scope guard (MVP)
Decides whether a request is covered by the calibration. Out-of-scope requests go to the strong model and are tagged `scope=out`.

- Hard rules: tools/function-calling, images/audio, `n > 1`, very long context beyond calibrated length, unsupported language (if calibration was English-only).
- Soft rule: embedding distance to the calibration set (for example, kNN distance above a threshold chosen on held-out data) as a lightweight OOD detector.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · 5.3 Provider layer (MVP)
chunks.heading: 5.3 Provider layer (MVP)
chunks.text:
5.3 Provider layer (MVP)
- `Provider` protocol: `async chat(request) -> Response | AsyncIterator[Chunk]`, usage accounting, normalized errors.
- One `OpenAICompatProvider` using `httpx.AsyncClient` (connection pooling, HTTP/2 where supported). Most hosted and local servers (OpenAI, OpenRouter, Together, Groq, vLLM, Ollama) speak this dialect, so one adapter covers both tiers.
- Timeouts (connect/first-byte/total), retry with exponential backoff and jitter on 429/5xx, per-provider circuit breaker.
- Cost accounting from a `pricing.yaml` (price per 1M input/output tokens, with an `as_of` date).

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · 5.7 Telemetry, storage and monitor (MVP → stretch)
chunks.heading: 5.7 Telemetry, storage and monitor (MVP → stretch)
chunks.text:
5.7 Telemetry, storage and monitor (MVP → stretch)
- Structured JSON logs (`structlog`) with a request id. **Prompt text is not stored by default**; only a hash and token counts. Full-text logging is opt-in per environment, and audit rows store text only when enabled.
- Metrics (Prometheus): request count by tier/scope/status, escalation rate, router latency histogram, TTFT and total latency by tier, token and estimated cost counters, audit count, rolling audited regret, drift statistics.
- Storage: SQLite (MVP), Postgres (stretch). Tables: `requests`, `audits`, `calibrations`.
- Drift monitor (periodic job): PSI/KS on the score distribution `s(X)` versus calibration, embedding-space drift (for example MMD or a domain-classifier AUC), and a rolling audited-regret estimate with a confidence interval. A breach flags the artifact as `suspect`, which can trigger recalibration or a fail-safe to a more conservative ε.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · 5.8 Semantic cache (stretch)
chunks.heading: 5.8 Semantic cache (stretch)
chunks.text:
5.8 Semantic cache (stretch)
A cache hit returns an earlier response, whose quality depends on the tier that produced it. Rules: high similarity threshold, cache key includes `(tier, params)`, cache disabled when measuring the guarantee, and a calibration-aware variant treated as part of the policy. The cache is a stretch precisely because it complicates the guarantee story.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · 5.9 Dashboard (MVP-lite)
chunks.heading: 5.9 Dashboard (MVP-lite)
chunks.text:
5.9 Dashboard (MVP-lite)
Streamlit app reading the DB: cost saved vs always-strong, escalation rate over time, audited regret with CI against ε, drift indicators, calibration history, and a "playground" showing score and route for a typed prompt. Grafana on Prometheus is a stretch.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · ARCHITECTURE.md · 7. Recalibration and drift (MVP → stretch)
chunks.heading: 7. Recalibration and drift (MVP → stretch)
chunks.text:
7. Recalibration and drift (MVP → stretch)
1. **Scheduled/triggered recalibration (MVP):** pool recent audit rows with the original calibration data (optionally recency-weighted), refit λ̂ with CRC, publish a new artifact, hot-reload.
2. **Weighted CRC under covariate shift (stretch):** estimate a density ratio `w(x)` with a domain classifier (calibration vs recent traffic) and use weighted CRC. Depends on the theory analysis in `SPLIT.md` (T4).
3. **Online threshold update (stretch):** `λ_{t+1} = clip(λ_t + η·(L_t − ε))`, an adaptive-conformal-style update that targets long-run average risk ε without exchangeability. Needs a bound derived and verified by the theory partner (T5) and audit labels.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · EVALUATION.md · 4. Data collection protocol
chunks.heading: 4. Data collection protocol
chunks.text:
4. Data collection protocol
1. Build the prompt pool; apply the dedup/split guard.
2. For each prompt run **both** models; store raw outputs, token counts, latency, finish reason, and `q` for each. Cache on `hash(prompt, model, params)`; make the job resumable.
3. Compute `regret_i`.
4. Freeze the dataset (hash it); record the hash in all downstream artifacts.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · EVALUATION.md · 5. Splits
chunks.heading: 5. Splits
chunks.text:
5. Splits
- Split by prompt hash into `D_router` (≈ 40%) and `D_pool` (≈ 60%).
- The router is trained **only** on `D_router`.
- Each guarantee experiment draws many random `(D_cal, D_test)` partitions from `D_pool`, scores them with the frozen router, and applies CRC on `D_cal`.
- For shift experiments, calibration comes from source domain(s) and test from held-out domain(s) (§8).

chunks.title: CertiRoute · EVALUATION.md · 10. Reproducibility
chunks.heading: 10. Reproducibility
chunks.text:
10. Reproducibility
- `make reproduce` runs from the frozen dataset to all figures/tables. Collection from APIs is separate (`make collect`) because it costs money and may not be bit-reproducible; the frozen paired-output dataset (or its hash and a download script, subject to licences) is the reproducibility anchor.
- All random seeds are in configs; each result JSON stores config, code git SHA, dataset hash, artifact id.
- Figures are generated by scripts, never by hand.

chunks.heading: G3 — ε sweep (reliability diagram)
chunks.text:
G3 — ε sweep (reliability diagram)
ε ∈ {0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20}. Plot target ε (x) vs mean realized risk (y) with CI and the `y = x` line. Expect points on or below the line. A large gap below the line quantifies conservativeness.

chunks.title: CertiRoute · EVALUATION.md · G6 — Negative controls (the guarantee is not magic)
chunks.heading: G6 — Negative controls (the guarantee is not magic)
chunks.text:
G6 — Negative controls (the guarantee is not magic)
| Control | Expected behavior |
|---|---|
| Fixed threshold `s > 0.5`, no calibration | No guarantee; risk varies with dataset and model pair |
| Threshold tuned on validation to hit ε empirically (no conformal correction) | Realized risk exceeds ε in a substantial fraction of splits, especially at small `n` |
| Calibrate on one domain, test on another (no mitigation) | Violation when the target is harder than the source |
| Router trained on `D_cal` (leakage) | Optimistic λ̂ and violation: demonstrates why D4 in `ARCHITECTURE.md` matters |

G8 — Label-noise sensitivity
Inject noise into `q` that mimics judge error (symmetric flips with rate η; or judge-specific confusion estimated on a labeled subset). Plot *true* risk (ground truth) vs ε for calibration done on noisy labels. This quantifies how judge error erodes the guarantee, and is a good theory question (`SPLIT.md`, T3).

|---|---|---|
| Always-strong | Upper-quality, highest cost | n/a |
| Always-cheap | Lowest cost, lowest quality | n/a |

Welcome to my Machine Learning training project! In this repository, I explore the **DBSCAN** (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) algorithm to cluster a dataset of heights and weights. The main goal of this project is to identify natural clusters and potential outliers in a dataset containing individuals' heights and weights. Unlike K-Means, which assumes spherical clusters, DBSCAN excels at finding arbitrarily shaped clusters and is robust to noise (outliers).

chunks.title: DBSCAN Clustering · README.md · 💡 Key Learnings
chunks.heading: 💡 Key Learnings
chunks.text:
💡 Key Learnings
- **Scaling is Crucial:** Density-based algorithms are highly sensitive to the scale of the features. Using `StandardScaler` was a vital preprocessing step.
- **Tuning `eps` and `min_samples`:** The success of DBSCAN heavily relies on finding the right epsilon and minimum samples. The Nearest Neighbors approach is a great way to estimate epsilon programmatically.
- **Outlier Detection:** One of the best features of DBSCAN is that it doesn't force every point into a cluster, allowing us to easily spot anomalies.

Why this document exists
This is not a "look how good my numbers are" summary. Several of the numbers below are worse than what was originally published. The point of this document is to show the *process* that found and fixed that — because in research, the ability to locate and honestly report findings that don't favor your own model is a stronger signal of quality than any single performance metric.

Everything here is independently verifiable against the codebase's own scripts, CSVs, and JSON outputs. Nothing is asserted without a script that reproduces it.

chunks.title: RAI-Axiom · axiom_audit_summary.md · The current, honest state of the results
chunks.heading: The current, honest state of the results
chunks.text:
The current, honest state of the results
- **Out-of-sample**: Axiom is statistically indistinguishable from a real-data-trained LSTM and from real SPY buy-and-hold, and significantly ahead of a real-data-trained XGBoost (though that gap shrinks substantially once seed correlation is properly accounted for).
- **Holdout (the genuinely unseen future window)**: Axiom is **behind** a simple Risk Parity rule, behind the LSTM baseline (now confirmed to be a trivial constant strategy) in every market where the difference is statistically significant, and behind real SPY by a large, if not fully statistically resolvable, margin.
- **The result does not generalize with confidence beyond the six markets tested** — this is stated explicitly in the project's own documentation, not left for a reader to discover.
- Two architectures were confounded in the project's history, meaning part of the improvement between an early published result and the current one cannot be cleanly attributed to more rigorous testing versus a genuinely different model.

None of this is a hidden failure. It is the current, fully disclosed, fully reproducible state of the evidence.

Programmed Mechanics (v0.1 - Milestones 1-4)
1.  **Abstract Entities:** Discrete or continuous resources that can be possessed, transformed, and exchanged.
2.  **Scarcity:** Entities have finite quantities.
3.  **Transformations (Relations):** Hardcoded rules that consume input entities to produce output entities.
4.  **Knowledge:** Abstract tokens required to execute certain transformations.
5.  **Partial Observation:** Agents only observe a subset of the world state (their own inventory and local knowledge).
6.  **Exchange:** Agents can voluntarily swap entities.
7.  **Relation Discovery:** Agents can randomly discover new transformations and the knowledge required to execute them.
8.  **Knowledge Diffusion:** Agents can share knowledge with other agents.
9.  **Utility (Implicit):** Agents will eventually (via RL) seek to maximize a utility function based on their preferences for specific entities.
10. **Time (Ticks):** The simulation progresses in discrete time steps.

chunks.title: RAI-Axiom · README.md · Limitations
chunks.heading: Limitations
chunks.text:
Limitations
1. **The LSTM baseline is a confirmed degenerate policy**: LSTM and XGBoost have been re-run across the same 10 seeds as Axiom after the seed-propagation fix (`scripts/baseline_multiseed.py`, 2026-08-29). The LSTM returns a *single distinct Sharpe* across all 10 seeds in 4 of 6 universes, and a direct per-day policy dump for 3 seeds (`scripts/lstm_degeneracy_check.py`) confirms **bit-identical weight vectors, constant over the entire window** — P(up) stays inside [0.549, 0.568] and never crosses the 0.5 threshold, so the arm is a static 80% equal-weight buy-and-hold. What Axiom Learned (Equity Universes)
In equity-class universes (US ETFs, US Mega-Cap, Global Indices), the Axiom policy exhibits:
- **Conservative allocation**: Higher cash fraction than Fast, reducing drawdowns
- **Multi-asset diversification**: Spreads weights across available assets rather than concentrating
- **Low turnover**: Rebalances infrequently (1–3 times per evaluation window), keeping cost impact minimal

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Every Axiom-vs-Fast comparison in this repo is a comparison of two different architectures, not
> two seeds or two checkpoints of one.** Axiom is `AxiomNet` (289,527 params, flatten over the 30-day
> window); Fast is `FastTradingNet` (51,703 params, mean-pool over time). They share no state_dict
> and a cross-load is rejected. This applies to the bullets above, the crypto-concentration forensics
> below, and the `[v6] Fast` column of the offset ablation. Any behavioural difference between them —
> including the crypto concentration failure — may reflect architecture, training run, or both, and
> this repo cannot separate the two: there is no `AxiomNet` checkpoint trained under Fast's recipe and
> no `FastTradingNet` checkpoint from the Kaggle run. Until 2026-08-29 both classes were named
> `DeepEndToEndTradingNet`, which is why earlier text treated them as one model.

chunks.heading: Interpreting the visuals
chunks.text:
Interpreting the visuals
- **Latest status and window compliance answer different questions.** A latest
  reading can pass even when earlier samples breached the target.
- **The composite score is sample compliance**, not contractual uptime.
- **The availability error budget estimates loss** from availability percentages
  over observed intervals. Telemetry gaps are excluded; this is not measured
  outage duration.
- **Heatmap cells show the share of failed metric checks** in each date/hour.
  Blank cells mean no samples.
- **Latency median and P95 describe sampled interval values**, not individual
  request latencies. Traffic bars show counts per interval, not requests/minute.
- **Threshold changes reuse the same telemetry.** A fixed simulation seed
  reproduces the scenario; refreshing advances the observation window.

chunks.heading: Google Cloud setup (optional)
chunks.text:
Google Cloud setup (optional)
1. Enable `monitoring.googleapis.com` in your Google Cloud project.
2. Configure Application Default Credentials or set
   `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` to your credential file path.
3. Grant the credential's account the `roles/monitoring.viewer` role.
4. Enter the project ID in the dashboard, or set `GCP_PROJECT_ID` or
   `GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT` before launch.
5. Select **Live GCP** in the sidebar.

The adapter reads uptime checks and Cloud Run request-count/latency metrics.
If Cloud Run request data is absent, it tries HTTPS load-balancer metrics. It
computes error rate from HTTP 5xx request counts, weights latency distribution
means by sample counts, and aligns observations by timestamp. Availability
shares the uptime-check observations in this integration.

Missing credentials, permissions, metric streams, or aligned coverage trigger a
clearly labeled **simulation fallback**. Missing data is never replaced with
invented healthy readings. Authenticated ingestion requires your own cloud
project and is not covered by local UI verification.

See the Google Cloud Monitoring metric catalog
for metric definitions.

chunks.title: Signal · README.md · How the analysis works
chunks.heading: How the analysis works
chunks.text:
How the analysis works
The core algorithm is **threshold-based SLA evaluation**. Each sampled reading
is compared with its configured target using an inclusive comparison:

| Metric | Default target | A sample passes when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uptime | 99.9% | Reading ≥ target |
| Response time | 200 ms | Reading ≤ target |
| Error rate | 0.1% | Reading ≤ target |
| Availability | 99.95% | Reading ≥ target |

Metric compliance (%) = passing samples / total samples × 100
Composite score (%)  = mean of the four metric compliance percentages
Violation deviation  = absolute difference between reading and target

**Example:** if 285 of 288 uptime samples meet the target, uptime compliance is
**98.96%**. If all four compliance scores are 98.96%, 100%, 97.22%, and 100%,
the composite is **99.05%**. This measures passing checks across the selected
window, separately from the latest reading.

Each failing metric reading becomes a violation record. Records are sorted by
timestamp and assigned a severity from their absolute deviation:
**Warning** below 0.05, **Moderate** from 0.05 to below 0.5, and **Critical** at
0.5 or above. These buckets use each metric's own units, so compare severity
within a metric.

Diagnostic observations use rules such as lowest compliance, business-hour
concentration, and gaps between violations. They guide investigation; they do
not establish root causes or use a trained machine-learning model.

chunks.title: VeraScan · README.md · MatchRecord Structure
chunks.heading: MatchRecord Structure
chunks.text:
MatchRecord Structure
Each match in `report.matches` contains:
- `eval_index: int` — Index of the sample in the evaluation dataset.
- `train_index: int` — Index of the sample in the training dataset.
- `eval_text: str` — Evaluation sample text.
- `train_text: str` — Matching training sample text.
- `score: float` — Similarity metric (`1.0` for exact matches, n-gram overlap ratio for ngram, Jaccard for fuzzy, cosine for semantic).
- `method: str` — Engine that produced the match (`"exact"`, `"ngram"`, `"fuzzy"`, `"semantic"`).

chunks.title: VeraScan · README.md · ⚠️ Limitations
chunks.heading: ⚠️ Limitations
chunks.text:
⚠️ Limitations
- **Large-Scale Semantic Search**: While FAISS provides fast approximate search, semantic matching encodes all samples using transformer models, which is compute-intensive on CPU for corpora with millions of rows. For very large datasets, start with `methods=["exact", "fuzzy"]`.
- **Character N-Gram Sensitivity**: Fuzzy matching relies on character 5-grams by default. Very short texts (fewer than 5 characters) fall back to exact matching.
- **Word N-Gram Length**: The `ngram` method needs at least `ngram_n` words (default 13) after cleaning; shorter eval texts produce no n-gram matches.
- **Cross-Lingual Matching**: The default semantic model (`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`) is optimized for English text. For multilingual evaluation datasets, specify a multilingual model via `model_name="paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2"`.

chunks.title: VeraScan · PyPI · MatchRecord Structure
chunks.heading: MatchRecord Structure
chunks.text:
MatchRecord Structure
Each match in `report.matches` contains:
- `eval_index: int` — Index of the sample in the evaluation dataset.
- `train_index: int` — Index of the sample in the training dataset.
- `eval_text: str` — Evaluation sample text.
- `train_text: str` — Matching training sample text.
- `score: float` — Similarity metric (`1.0` for exact matches, n-gram overlap ratio for ngram, Jaccard for fuzzy, cosine for semantic).
- `method: str` — Engine that produced the match (`"exact"`, `"ngram"`, `"fuzzy"`, `"semantic"`).

chunks.title: VeraScan · PyPI · ⚠️ Limitations
chunks.heading: ⚠️ Limitations
chunks.text:
⚠️ Limitations
- **Large-Scale Semantic Search**: While FAISS provides fast approximate search, semantic matching encodes all samples using transformer models, which is compute-intensive on CPU for corpora with millions of rows. For very large datasets, start with `methods=["exact", "fuzzy"]`.
- **Character N-Gram Sensitivity**: Fuzzy matching relies on character 5-grams by default. Very short texts (fewer than 5 characters) fall back to exact matching.
- **Word N-Gram Length**: The `ngram` method needs at least `ngram_n` words (default 13) after cleaning; shorter eval texts produce no n-gram matches.
- **Cross-Lingual Matching**: The default semantic model (`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`) is optimized for English text. For multilingual evaluation datasets, specify a multilingual model via `model_name="paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2"`.
